nodes.title: The use case
widgets_values:
WHERE IS MY ASSET IN THIS PLATE?
You have the asset's mesh (the 'Load 3D (Advanced)' node) and a shot that contains it, but not the placement - the plate came from another tool, another artist, or a generation step that kept only pixels. What it does come with is DEPTH. 'CV PPF Pose Estimation' hashes oriented point PAIRS of the model and lets the depth cloud's pairs vote for the 4x4 that maps model -> scene: no markers, no texture, no initial guess, and the ground plane in the scene does not disturb the vote. The answer is COARSE (9.2 degrees out here), so 'CV ICP Register' polishes it and 'CV Matrix Multiply' composes the two - 1.0 degrees, 0.08 m.
THE POSE IS THE PRODUCT. The rows below spend it: 'CV Rasterize Mesh' re-renders the mesh at the recovered pose into a silhouette + depth pair that lines up with the plate pixel for pixel - the silhouette is an inpaint mask for re-texturing that object as it stands, and the depth is METRIC camera-space Z, so its preview is DARK where the object is NEAR. A depth ControlNet wants the opposite (near = bright, normalized), which is the convention the 'depth' MASK of 'CV Preview 3D (Calibrated Camera)' already uses - invert this one before conditioning on it. 'CV Camera Pose To 3D View' turns the same pose into a camera, so a SECOND asset drops into the plate with the same perspective; and 'CV Write PLY' shows the fit in 3D.
ADAPTING IT: the depth here is RENDERED, which is what gives the graph a ground truth to score against. Replace the 'depth_metric' of 'CV Preview 3D (Calibrated Camera)' with a real RGB-D capture, the stereo reprojection of workflow 86, or a monocular depth model, and nothing downstream changes.

nodes.title: Why the graph is wired this way
widgets_values:
THREE THINGS THIS GRAPH IS SHAPED AROUND, all measured on it:
1. NORMALS DECIDE THE ANSWER, and a plane fit is not good enough for the model. 'CV Point Cloud Normals' fits a plane through each point's neighbours, which leaves the SIGN arbitrary - fine for the scene, where 'flip toward viewpoint' orients everything at the camera, but a closed model has no viewpoint to flip towards. Feed PPF a plane-fit model cloud and it answers 177-179 degrees out, consistently. 'CV Mesh Vertex Normals' takes them from the TRIANGLE WINDING instead: 9.2 degrees.
2. HANDEDNESS, TWICE. 'CV Depth to 3D Points' NEGATES Y (its cloud is meant for the Y-up viewer), so it arrives MIRRORED relative to the camera frame the mesh and the pose live in - and a mirrored cloud has no pose to find. One 'CV Flip Axis (3D)' undoes it. Going back out to the viewer for 'CV Write PLY' needs BOTH Y and Z negated - a 180-degree turn about X - and negating either one ALONE is a reflection, which the viewer draws quite happily while showing you the far side of the object. Measured here: the +X flank of the truck faces the camera in the shot (mean z 10.9 against 12.3), and this graph shipped for a day with only the Y flip, showing the -X flank. That is why the step is now ONE node, 'CV Convert Axis Convention (3D)', which names both spaces instead of leaving you to count minus signs - the cloud-level counterpart of the axis_convention on 'CV Mesh From 3D Model'.
3. ICP DIVERGES rather than degrading when it runs out of points. Each pyramid level halves the cloud, and a partial scene (one face of the object, plus clutter that is not the object) starves the coarse levels: 6 levels diverge here, 4 converge. cv2 signals that with a 1e10 residual while still returning 0 from registerModelToScene - the node turns that into found=false, and num_levels is the knob to lower when you see it.

nodes.title: The control rows, and how to score this
widgets_values:
WHAT THE CONTROL ROWS ARE FOR.
Same ICP, same settings, started from the model's own frame instead of the PPF pose. It does not refuse: it slides the truck flat onto the ground plane, 63 degrees and 3.3 m from the truth, and reports found=true with a residual of 0.0028 - SIX TIMES BETTER than the 0.017 of the run that actually found the object. That is the sharpest thing this graph has to say about ICP: its residual measures how well the points it kept agree, not whether it is looking at the right object, so it can never tell you that. And it is what the global matcher buys - PPF is not a better ICP, it is the only thing here that finds the object at all.
THE TWO FAILURE ROWS say different things, and the difference is worth knowing. Feed the BARE GROUND - a scene the object is simply not in - and PPF does not refuse: it returns a pose, found=true, on about a sixth of the votes the real match gets. There is no 'not found' for a cloud that is merely wrong, so the votes and the scores below are the only thing between you and a confident answer about nothing. What cv2 genuinely cannot do is a cloud with NO EXTENT ALONG Z - a wall square-on to the camera, every point at the same depth. That throws 'Unknown C++ exception' inside cv2, and the node turns it into found=false with an identity pose and an empty pose stack instead of halting the workflow. (A floor is a plane too and cv2 takes it happily: flatness is not the problem, zero depth range is.)
SCORING. The three nearest-distance readouts do rank the stages (median 0.30 coarse -> 0.20 refined -> 0.55 for the un-initialized run), and unlike the ICP residual they are not fooled. But on a one-view scene WITH CLUTTER they are blunt: the model's unseen far side finds the ground plane whatever the pose, so the margins are small. The silhouette IoU is the score that matches the use case - it asks whether the conditioning mask lands on the object, which is the only question the downstream ControlNet cares about.
